headline: The Fed said “we’ll see”. The two-year auction said 4.787%.
standfirst: Tuesday was quiet on the surface — the S&P 500 lost 0.06 points to 7,764.64, the Nasdaq added 0.45% to a second straight record at 27,244.28, the Dow fell 0.36% — and busy underneath. Treasury sold $69 billion of two-year notes at 4.787%, the highest stop since May 2024 and 58bp above August's; Brent settled at $99.25, its first close under $100 since 9 September, and has kept falling overnight; and four Fed officials, none of them voters this year, all pointed the same way. Today brings the first activity data since the hike — flash PMIs for the euro area at 04:00 ET, the UK at 04:30 and the US at 09:45 — a $70 billion five-year auction at 13:00, and Xi Jinping's arrival in Washington.

bullets.title: The market took the two-year paper. It just charged 58bp more for it.
bullets.text: The $69 billion two-year auction stopped at 4.787% against 4.204% in August, the highest yield Treasury has paid on the maturity since May 2024. Demand was fine: bid-to-cover 2.63 against a 2.61 six-auction average, a tail of 0.2bp, indirect bidders at 57.79% against a 58.6% average, and the Fed's own SOMA account taking $10.4 billion non-competitively. Cash closes barely moved — the two-year at 4.749%, the ten-year at 4.966%, the thirty-year at 5.302% — and one-year inflation swaps have slipped to 2.3% from 2.6% a fortnight ago on the oil move. Five-years today (last stop 4.393%), seven-years Thursday (4.512%).

bullets.title: Six sessions of oil, and the physical market still says the other thing
bullets.text: WTI's October contract settled at $94.59 and Brent at $99.25, then both kept falling overnight — the November WTI contract is near $89, Brent near $98.4 — for a sixth straight decline. The drivers are diplomatic and logistical: Saudi Arabia has begun testing its East–West pipeline and could resume exports from Yanbu within days; Trump told the UN he faces a “big decision” between a deal with Iran and annihilating it, said a deal was likely after the 3 November midterms, then said US officials had a “very good” three-hour meeting with Iran's delegation. Iran has reportedly offered to reopen Hormuz within seven days if the US lifts its blockade on Iranian ports; the Revolutionary Guards then added Yemen to the list. Against all that: tanker tracking showed only two merchant ships through the strait on Monday, diesel is at record highs in Europe and the US, the API reported a 1.8 million barrel build against a draw expected, and Treasury is reported to be studying a diesel export ban. Tighter US sanctions on Iranian aviation take effect today.

bullets.title: Four Fed speakers, no votes, one direction
bullets.text: Richmond's Barkin: “Will additional hikes be required, and how many? We'll see.” He said more than 60% of the PCE basket was rising faster than 3% in July, that “passing” shocks are not proving short-lived, and that the economy is if anything firming — defence, manufacturing, bank loan pipelines. Boston's Collins backed the September hike and flagged “an increased likelihood of future scenarios in which inflation remains notably above 2%”, arguing for a “somewhat more restrictive” rate. Williams defended policy and gave no guidance; Jefferson spoke on the discount window. On Monday Goolsbee said the Fed could no longer look through supply shocks and Musalem said further hikes may be needed. None of the six votes in 2026; Barkin does next year. Futures put 28 October at about 55% and December near 89%, and 16 of 18 officials projected at least one more hike this year. The dollar index closed at 100.60, and the greenback hit its highest since late July against the Canadian dollar.

bullets.title: A record close with more new lows than new highs
bullets.text: On Monday, more S&P 500 stocks set 52-week lows than 52-week highs — the first time that has happened on a record-setting day since December 1999. Tuesday kept the shape: the Nasdaq's second straight record came with the Magnificent Seven index down 0.23%, Amazon off 1.34%, Alphabet 1.07%, Microsoft 0.72%, Meta 0.63%. The bid moved to memory — Micron rose 5% and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index 2.06% — and financials fell 1.97% as the large banks sold off. The Richmond Fed survey printed −2 against +5 expected. KB Home reported housing revenue down 20% on 19% fewer deliveries at a $473,000 average price, with the first year-on-year rise in backlog in four years. FactSet has S&P 500 earnings growing about 29% for the quarter now ending, a third straight quarter above 25% — the reason the index is 0.4% from its high with the ten-year at 4.97%.

bullets.title: Xi lands today. The truce he is here about expires in November.
bullets.text: Xi Jinping arrives at Joint Base Andrews today for a three-day state visit — Trump is meeting him on the tarmac — with the bilateral on Thursday and a state dinner that evening to which Bezos, Musk, Pichai, Dell, Huang, Altman, Fraser and Cook have been invited. The agenda is the one-year trade truce that expires in November, export controls, rare earths and AI policy; Bessent and Vice Premier He Lifeng did the preparatory work on Monday. Both sides are described as wanting stability and spectacle over deliverables. Hong Kong opened flat and Shanghai mixed on it. Tokyo is shut for a second day for Silver Week, the Kospi rose about 1%, and the Australian dollar is under pressure after Bullock said upside inflation risks could materialise from energy and that she is not signalling the 29 September decision.

calendar.event: Flash PMIs: Germany 03:30, euro area 04:00, UK 04:30 (September)
calendar.note: Euro-area manufacturing seen 52.7 after 52.7, services 51.7 after 51.6; UK manufacturing 51.4 after 51.7, services 52.0 after 52.5. Both central banks are in hiking mode, so a firm print is hawkish rather than good.

Manufacturing seen 53.5 after 53.9, services 56.0 after 56.5, composite 56.0. The first activity data since the hike, a day after the Richmond Fed survey missed at −2. The prices-paid lines matter more than the headlines.
Fifth Fed speaker in two days. Every non-voter so far has leaned toward more; the Chair has said nothing.
A 0.6 million barrel draw expected after the API's 1.8 million build. With crude down six sessions, a second build would be the first physical number to agree with the price.
Previous stop 4.393%; the five-year is 4.83%. After Tuesday's two-year the question is not whether it clears but at what tail.

calendar.event: Xi Jinping arrives in Washington; Iran aviation sanctions take effect
calendar.note: Arrival ceremony at Andrews today, the bilateral and state dinner Thursday. Any line on the trade truce or AI policy trades semis first.

calendar.event: Jobless claims; SNB 03:30; Australia jobs (Wed 21:30 ET); $44bn seven-year 13:00
calendar.note: Claims seen 201,000 after 196,000, marked down from 203,000. Australia is seen adding 20,000 jobs at 4.5% unemployment ahead of the RBA on Monday. The SNB is expected to hold at zero.
Durable goods now seen −0.4% after +1.1%, ex-transport +0.6%, core capital goods +0.5% off a July revised to flat. Michigan sentiment 47.6, one-year inflation expectations 4.6%.

sessionNote: The overnight tape has extended Tuesday rather than reversed it. WTI's November contract is down about 1.5% near $89.2 and Brent 0.9% near $98.4 at 01:00 ET, a sixth session; the dollar index is near 100.7; Bitcoin is $86,721, up 0.61%, having taken back Tuesday's dip; gold is flat at $4,375. US futures were within 0.03% of unchanged at 20:45 ET. Tokyo is closed, Hong Kong opened flat, the Kospi rose about 1%. The day has a shape: Europe's PMIs print before New York opens, the US flash at 09:45 is the first activity read since the hike, and the five-year at 13:00 is the second of three auctions into a curve the two-year sale just repriced. The clean window is the US morning; the risk is a headline out of Washington or New York — Xi's arrival, an Iran line — landing on top of the auction.
watchOut: Reading six down days in crude as a settlement, and reading $89 WTI as a $5 crash. The first: Brent has fallen about $10 since last Tuesday on pipeline tests, a three-hour meeting and a tanker count, while the evidence from the physical market points the other way — two merchant ships through Hormuz on Monday, diesel at record highs, an API build, and a president whose own timeline puts a deal after 3 November. Saxo's Ole Hansen does not see much further downside until refined-product flows actually increase. The second: WTI's front month rolled from October to November overnight, and the October contract settled at $94.59 — the gap between the two is the market paying up for barrels now, not a fall. A short-energy position sized for the headline is sized for the roll.

archive.headline: An App Store ranking moved a trillion dollars
archive.summary: Meta's Muse agent topped the US iPhone chart and the CPU complex repriced around it: Meta +11.43%, AMD +9.95% to a first $1 trillion close, Intel +12%, Arm +17%, and the Nasdaq to its first record since June. Crude fell to an eleven-day low on Hormuz shipping data and the ten-year came back under 5%, into a $69 billion two-year auction.

archive.headline: The war premium leaks out before the UN
archive.summary: Monday with no US data and a live diplomatic wire. Crude fell for a fourth session as traders priced a chance of US–Iran contact at the UN General Assembly and Saudi Arabia worked to restore its East–West pipeline, with the ten-year coming into the day at 5.01% after its first close above 5% since July 2007.

archive.headline: The hike landed. The bond market blinked first.
archive.summary: Weekend edition. The Fed's unanimous 25bp on Wednesday took the Dow down 631 points and Thursday gave most of it back, with the S&P up 1.14% to 7,637.76 as the ten-year fell to 4.93% and oil slid. The weekend risk was the Iran war, with Trump saying he was near a decision on resuming large-scale strikes.

archive.headline: The ten-year touched 5% into the decision. The hike is not the event.
archive.summary: FOMC day. The 10-year had closed at 5.00% after touching 5.04%, the highest since 2007, with a 25bp hike priced at 92–94%. WTI had jumped 5.1% to $106.56 as fighting intensified in the Middle East; every US sector but energy closed red on Tuesday.

archive.headline: Core CPI ran hot into an FOMC that is now 90% priced to hike
archive.summary: Weekend edition. Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected, PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year, and September hike odds moved from 61% to about 90%. Equities closed the week higher regardless — S&P +0.86% Friday, VIX −11% — while the 10-year finished at 4.96%.

archive.headline: Core CPI at a four-month high, hike odds jump to ~90%
archive.summary: Headline CPI held at 3.4% year-over-year but core rose 0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected. Energy added 2.1% and gasoline 3.9%; airline fares rose 2.7%. Equities rallied regardless — S&P +0.86%, VIX −11% — while the 10-year touched 4.97%.

archive.headline: PPI beats, ECB hikes to 2.50%
archive.summary: August PPI came in at 5.4% year-over-year against 5.3% expected with July revised up from flat. The ECB raised its deposit rate 25bp to 2.50% effective 16 September and cut its 2028 inflation forecast to 2.1%. September hike odds moved from 61% to 72%.
